items.originalTitle: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
items.author: Morgan Jerkins
items.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
items.summary: The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here. In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New York living, he pursues Lisa, the heiress to a different kind of throne – that of a fast-food business called McDowell’s. The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but arrogant fiance? Will their families accept their Lisa and Akeem if they do decide to marry? Spoiler alert: there’s a happy ending. The plot progression is simple but the character development is full of heart and candor.

items.title: ‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off
items.summary: As we come to the end of another series, former contestants including Kim-Joy, Syabira Yusoff and Christiaan de Vries reminisce on their time in the tent – and the aftermath The Great British Bake Off is just about to finish its best season in years. Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing. We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. The scale runs from “a very nice level of X-list celebrity” to “a better version of me”, with a lot of life lessons (and a fart corner) along the way.

items.originalTitle: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
items.author: Peter Bradshaw
items.title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
items.summary: Nicolas Wadimoff invites refugees to draw a floor plan of their former neighbourhood, bringing raw and agonising pain to the surface A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza. In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.) The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewee talks of attending the Edward Said conservatory , now rubble; another talks of her work in film-making and animation. Another man plays poignantly beautiful music on his qanun, a type of zither, and then specifies the point in the music at which he was showered with glass from an explosion while he was playing it in Gaza.

items.title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
items.summary: Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar . The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight. Gohar describes the chandelier , made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It joins a long list of extravagant yet still edible installations she has created, including lifesize armchairs made of brioche , an entire room constructed with Belgian chocolate and a four-metre-long mortadella that had to be lifted into the party’s venue using a crane.

As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. items.originalTitle: License-Plate Readers Are Accelerating ICE’s Crackdown
items.title: License-Plate Readers Are Accelerating ICE’s Crackdown
items.summary: S unday is usually a slow day for ICE. There are fewer officers on duty. The people they want to arrest are more likely to stay indoors. The agency’s arrest numbers tend to dip, and that can put pressure on the officers working a Sunday shift. This appears to have been the case on September 20 in Austin, when an ICE officer identified in court filings as D.F. pulled up behind a blue Toyota Corolla around midday. The car was parked outside a restaurant with its hazard lights flashing—a telltale sign of a delivery driver making a pickup. Officer D.F., who was driving an unmarked SUV, pointed his automated license-plate reader at the Corolla. D.F. learned that the vehicle was registered to Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan with a pending deportation order. D.F. and his partner that day, identified as L.G., attempted to stop and question Garcés Pérez, but he drove away, clipping L.G. with his side mirror. The officers pursued the Corolla, and when L.G. tried to stop the vehicle a second time, he drew his weapon and shot Garcés Pérez in the back. (L.G. was not using a body camera , in violation of ICE policy, and the sequence of events immediately leading up to the gunfire was not recorded.) Garcés Pérez survived, but he has been charged with assaulting a federal officer and remains in custody. During a federal-court hearing 10 days later, the Department of Homeland Security special agent Rick Bazan, who investigated the shooting, testified that D.F. and L.G. were “doing random checks on vehicles and at random places” that Sunday. The officers were looking for people they could arrest, Bazan said in an audio recording of the proceeding obtained by Austin’s KUT News , describing those tactics as routine. The shooting was one of several in recent months that have generated outrage over ICE’s use of force during vehicle stops. Officers fatally shot a 52-year-old contractor named Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston on July 7, and an ICE officer in Maine killed another delivery driver, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in his car six days later. Plate readers were used by officers in both incidents, a senior ICE official told me. The killings, and other shootings since, prompted ICE leaders to order more training and require the use of body cameras. But the agency has already placed powerful new technologies into officers’ hands and encouraged their aggressive deployment. It’s hard to see how the agency will be able to satisfy White House demands for more arrests while telling officers to use more restraint with their potent new tools. I CE started deploying license-plate readers nearly a decade ago. The technology was primarily reserved for criminal-investigation teams performing tasks such as tracking suspected drug smugglers. Law-enforcement agencies have generally found broad public support for the use of surveillance technologies when they’re used to catch dangerous criminals. Concerns about privacy and mass surveillance tend to arise when the government uses the technology for nonviolent offenses such as immigration violations. DHS’s civil-rights and civil-liberties officers have tried to limit the use of these tools by warning about the risk of privacy violations. According to a “Privacy Impact Assessment” published by the department in 2022, the use of plate readers is prohibited for “ad hoc” queries and to initiate traffic stops solely on the basis of a search result. The assessment said that ICE must limit use of the plate readers to officers with appropriate training, and require them to state a justification when using the technology. ICE is also required to maintain logs that are subject to quarterly internal audits. During the Biden administration, officers had to get supervisory approval to use the plate readers, a veteran ICE official told me, and officers were not authorized to do vehicle stops “except under very limited circumstances that would have necessitated that they KNEW who was in the car,” the official said. (This official, like others I spoke with, did so on the condition of anonymity because they’re not authorized to talk with reporters.) After immigration-enforcement officers shot and killed two U.S. citizens during the ICE crackdown in Minneapolis in January, the White House asked its “border czar,” Tom Homan, to calm tensions and shift tactics. Homan, who worked for many years at ICE, said officers would return to the “targeted enforcement” approach that the agency has traditionally employed. In practice, that meant fewer raids on Home Depot parking lots and more traffic stops. The plate readers helped ICE ramp up everywhere, but less visibly, one vehicle at a time. ICE did not respond to my questions about the expanded use of the automated plate readers. But Trump-administration officials have repeatedly said they have a duty to intensify immigration enforcement because the Biden administration allowed dangerous migrants to enter the United States en masse without proper screening. [ Read: ICE after the blowout ] Over the past several months, ICE has been piloting a new license-plate-reader mobile app that syncs with the agency’s databases, including its powerful new mapping tool, ELITE (Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement), which was developed by Palantir, the technology company. ICE officials I’ve spoken with say that ELITE has the ability to synthesize many of the databases they used to check one by one, potentially allowing them to quickly see phone numbers and addresses, motor-vehicle records, federal immigration files, Medicaid data, criminal records, and biometric information. Officers can simply point their phone at a license plate and pull up an individual’s case file and photo in a way that one ICE official likened to looking at a baseball card. A positive match in the ELITE system remains in the officers’ user history for 30 days, and searches that do not result in a match are deleted within 72 hours. Senior ICE leaders have been taking steps to rein in the use of the plate readers, perhaps in anticipation of increased oversight from incoming Democratic majorities in Congress. The agency has been developing new operation procedures to prohibit officers from using the plate readers to go “fishing” for targets at random, the way D.F. and L.G. used the devices, three ICE officials told me. Officers will likely be instructed to use the plate readers only as verification tools for subjects they’re already pursuing. But those guidelines have not been finalized or distributed. I CE remains under daily pressure from White House officials—especially Stephen Miller, the new chief of staff —to capture and deport as many people as possible, despite the administration’s claims that it is focused on “the worst of the worst.” The push to maximize arrests has resulted in a workplace culture in which officers are more likely to get in trouble for not taking action than they are for acting too aggressively, veteran officials have told me. ICE deported more than 483,000 people during the 2026 fiscal year, which ended September 30, the Department of Homeland Security announced this month. That is the highest one-year total ever, although it is still short of the administration’s goal of 1 million deportations a year. The ICE officials I spoke with said that arrests remain near record levels, at about 50,000 a month, and deportations are exceeding 42,000 a month. Traffic stops are essential to ICE’s arrest goals as the agency relies less on the tactic known as “knock and talk,” in which officers arrive at a subject’s residence and try to convince the person to open the door. ICE officers generally cannot force their way into a home without a warrant signed by a judge, and advocacy organizations have spread the word not to open doors for ICE, no matter how persuasive officers may be. Vehicles do not offer individuals the same constitutional privacy protections as homes do—which is one reason for the proliferation of videos showing ICE officers smashing car windows of drivers who disobey orders. Even in instances when ICE knows the address of a person they’re seeking to arrest, officers now typically wait until the person is in their car before attempting to apprehend them. [ Read: ICE has quietly changed its deadly-force rule ] The license-plate readers also help shield the agency from accusations of racial profiling. To initiate a vehicle stop, ICE officers must be able to articulate a “reasonable suspicion” that the individual is unlawfully present in the country. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a September 2025 opinion supporting the ability of federal agents and officers to use factors such as language and ethnic appearance when establishing reasonable suspicion, and such street-level checks are now known colloquially now as “ Kavanaugh stops .” When officers use plate readers, they’re leaving it to the technology to determine whom to pull over and check. ELITE creates neighborhood heat maps that show officers where they have the best chances of finding immigrants with deportation orders or criminal records, and others potentially subject to ICE arrest. ICE officers face a low risk of disciplinary action for initiating a stop on the basis of a license-plate-reader hit if they’re in a target-rich neighborhood that has a high percentage of immigrants subject to arrest, current and former ICE officials told me. They were skeptical that new guidelines on the use of the readers would curb their indiscriminate use, because of that low risk of disciplinary action. One former DHS official who worked on privacy issues likened the license-plate readers to a digital version of “stop-and-frisk,” allowing officers to go to immigrant neighborhoods and run checks on drivers who don’t appear white. Peter Mina, a former ICE attorney who was the deputy officer of the DHS Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, told me that the office’s oversight role has been weakened since President Trump returned for a second term. Working through the constitutional considerations involved in the use of new technologies such as automated plate readers is “the whole point of having a civil-rights office,” Mina said, and the technology “creates the potential for rampant civil-rights and civil-liberties abuses.” “I can’t imagine that all of a sudden someone in the chain of command is going to start monitoring and disciplining people, or counseling them, because they are indiscriminately using license-plate readers,” Mina said. “Because they’re probably feeling the same pressure to produce.” T he most extensive AI-powered plate-reader network in the United States is operated by Flock Safety, a company that has tried to cultivate a reputation for providing a neutral crime-fighting tool by avoiding controversial clients, including ICE. But lawmakers and privacy advocates have alleged that Flock cameras are being used by police agencies trying to investigate abortions as well as by ICE officers looking for immigrants—claims that the company denies. Flock is already facing a backlash in some cities and states, including Texas, where Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa ran a campaign ad showing her as a rifle-toting video-game character shooting down the cameras. The state has installed more than 10,000 plate readers linked to the Flock database, which is designed to provide law-enforcement officers with real-time location data on subjects they’re pursuing. Courtney Terlecki, a spokesperson for Flock, wrote to me that the company “is the only major license plate reader provider without a contract with the Department of Homeland Security.” Terlecki said the company provides customers with filters to block searches related to immigration enforcement, and every search must include a specified offense type and is recorded in an audit log. Critics of the surveillance technology say that ICE has found an easy work-around. Chad Marlow, a senior policy counsel at the ACLU, told me the group obtained records showing thousands of instances in which ICE officers had asked local and state police agencies to run searches of Flock data on their behalf. ICE says it has more than 2,600 agreements with state and local jurisdictions under the agency’s 287(g) program, up from 135 when Trump took office last year. Those partnerships are concentrated in Texas, Florida, and other southern states. According to Marlow, state and local police departments that partner with ICE have learned to avoid including terms such as immigration in their search logs. “We have seen searches where the ‘reason for the investigation’ put in was investigation , or hehehe , or LOL ,” Marlow told me. “There are no actual speed bumps within the system.” Communities had previously accepted the widespread deployment of plate-reader cameras on the premise of improved public safety, not civil immigration enforcement, Marlow added. Terlecki said that Flock customers “own their data and retain full control over it, including whether and with whom it is shared.” Last month, nearly three dozen lawmakers sent a letter to ICE Acting Director David Venturella objecting to what they called “side-door” access to the national network of Flock plate readers. The lawmakers said, “Chilling, unrestrained surveillance obtained without judicial authorization, contractual safeguards, or public transparency, represents far more than a procedural lapse—it represents the quiet expansion of a federal surveillance system operating out of sight and beyond any meaningful public oversight.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] The lawmakers told ICE they wanted a detailed breakdown by November 20 indicating how many times immigration officers had accessed Flock databases, how the data were used, and what other automated-plate-reader systems ICE is using. Representative Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, has proposed legislation to curb ICE’s use of facial-recognition software and other AI-powered apps. And he has pledged to conduct aggressive oversight of ICE when the Democratic majority takes control of Congress in January. His committee and others will be busy. Democrats have said they plan to investigate fatal shootings involving ICE officers conducting traffic stops, as well as the agency’s hiring surge last spring, its spending on detention centers and deportation flights, and allegations of inhumane conditions inside ICE facilities. With so much to choose from, it’s difficult to predict where license-plate readers may rank on their priority list.

items.originalTitle: Have Wisconsin Democrats previously pursued ranked-choice voting?
items.author: Hope Karnopp / Milwaukee Journal Sentinel
items.title: Have Wisconsin Democrats previously pursued ranked-choice voting?
items.summary: Reading Time: minute Wisconsin Watch partners with Gigafact to produce Fact Briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims. Yes. In each legislative session since 2019, groups of Wisconsin Democrats supported some version of ranked-choice voting, in which voters mark candidates in order of preference. One 2026 bill would have required ranked-choice voting for federal, state and local elections. Another proposal would have allowed local governments to opt in. Both had around 20 Democrats listed in support. One version , called “Final-Five Voting,” received bipartisan support and got a public hearing in 2021. Some Republicans supported a constitutional amendment that would have banned ranked-choice voting in Wisconsin, but it didn’t advance. Only Alaska and Maine use ranked-choice voting statewide; some U.S. cities use it. Wisconsin’s new Democratic leaders haven’t listed ranked-choice voting among their first priorities , though it could be taken up. Instead, lawmakers have focused on a plan to give the state’s electoral votes to the popular vote winner in presidential races. This Fact Brief is responsive to conversations such as this one . Sources Wisconsin State Legislature: SB 1130 Wisconsin State Legislature: SB 594 Wisconsin State Legislature: Hearing Materials for SB250 Wisconsin State Legislature: 2023 AJR 101 National Conference of State Legislatures: Ranked Choice Voting Milwaukee Journal Sentinel: Democratic legislative leaders vow aggressive agenda in new majority Have Wisconsin Democrats previously pursued ranked-choice voting? is a post from Wisconsin Watch , a non-profit investigative news site covering Wisconsin since 2009. items.originalTitle: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
items.author: Paul Sullivan
items.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
items.summary: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein.

items.summary: The folding iPhone is early-adopter gold, changing the way iOS works and successfully condensing a tablet into your pocket, but it is not for everyone Apple’s first folding phone has upended the usual order of things with some interesting choices about how you use a iPhone – for better or worse. The Duo sits atop the pile as Apple’s most expensive smartphone – at £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499) it costs more than most of its folding Android rivals and as much as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the latest iPad mini combined.

items.originalTitle: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know
items.author: Anna Gordon
items.title: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know
items.summary: Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically. This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event. Jenna Heritage: ‘Everyone’s big fear is that they are going to die in pain’

items.originalTitle: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week
items.author: Rachel Aroesti, Hollie Richardson and Alexi Duggins
items.title: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week
items.summary: The Hollywood star is joined by celebrity guests as she shares ‘practical tips’. Plus, David Cameron’s deeply personal series about Alzheimer’s The second podcast from her wellness empire is ostensibly centred on Paltrow’s incredibly niche lifestyle advice: where to eat the “best cacio e pepe in Rome”, for example, or “whether it’s weird to use an obsidian gua sha tool on a plane”. In reality, the show is a weekly cosy chat with a showbiz pal (first up, Zoe Saldaña) peppered with a few practical tips – such as how to eat enough protein if you can’t face any more eggs. Rachel Aroesti Widely available, episodes weekly
